extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; general readers interested in 19th-century US press
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of mid‑19th century American newspapers (Greeley/Tribune, Raymond/Times, southern press), their editorial policies, social influence, and the political context that shaped press development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative political stance; careful accuracy; avoid reforms/sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Raymond planned a paper that would be "conservative in politics, carefully accurate in its news, and without 'reforms or sensations.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains this as the explicit editorial standard for the new Times: cautious political posture, factual care in news reporting, and deliberate avoidance of reformist agitation or sensationalism — intended to attract moderates between more radical and more sensational papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, crisp, critical and humorous editorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Dana believed "Weed's short, crisp editorial articles, critical and humorous, were the kind that would be most popular."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This articulates an editorial-style criterion: brevity, crispness, wit and critical tone in unsigned/lead editorials as a popular and effective format for a successful paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penny journalism (cheap price) to reach the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: The "introduction of penny journalism... eventually made the question of slavery the one that held the North as a political unit" and was "one of the important steps that led to the spread of journalism among the masses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low-cost (penny) pricing and mass circulation are presented as a strategic/structural criterion for expanding press influence and politicizing broad public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide social and institutional penetration as measure of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The weekly Tribune "had become the great anti-slavery journal, and 'went into almost every parsonage, college, and farmer's home in the Northern states.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paper's influence is judged by its penetration into diverse social institutions and households — presence in churches, colleges, and farms is presented as evidence of national reach and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigorous political advocacy/whole‑souled engagement builds fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Greeley achieved greatest fame "by his vigorous championship of the Free Soil party and by the whole-souled manner in which he later threw himself into the Republican party."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active, wholehearted partisan advocacy is presented as a criterion by which an editor/newspaper gains national influence and recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing important political speeches/content increases circulation and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: When Seward's speech was printed in the weekly Tribune "the circulation rose to 162,000 copies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting and printing consequential political speeches or documents is an editorial decision with measurable audience and influence benefits; inclusion of such content is an evaluative lever for newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial openness to controversial/intellectual movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Greeley "open[ed] his columns to the socialists of that day. Fourier... presented Fourier's ideas to the public in a series of articles, which ran for two or three years in the Tribune."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Welcoming controversial or avant-garde ideas in regular columns is presented as a characteristic of intellectually influential papers and a way to attract reformist contributors and readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of public discussion and independence from autocratic/material control
rubrics_metrics.description: "There can be no idealists, no great editors or journals, where brute force and material wealth so completely control," — used to explain southern press backwardness under slaveholder autocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A free public sphere and editorial independence from concentrated material/political power are described as necessary conditions for the development of notable editors and journals; suppression by elites is a structural anti‑criterion that prevents vibrant journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inflammatory regional interference; cautious respect for other local institutions/prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Raymond declared the Times would not "countenance any improper interference on the part of the people of one locality with the institutions, or even the prejudices, of any other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This editorial rule—avoid provoking other regions' institutions/prejudices—is offered as an intentional policy of temperate discussion and regional sensitivity, though the text also notes limits of purely temperate approaches in resolving deep moral conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic audience positioning between extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Raymond sought "a paper that would be less radical, less addicted to all the 'isms'... that would appeal to those who thought Greeley extreme and Bennett impossible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate editorial positioning to attract the centrist/moderate audience (between perceived extremes) is presented as a strategy for building readership and political influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers as educational factors (economic and moral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charles Francis Adams said "The New York Tribune... was the greatest educational factor, economically and morally, this country has ever known."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond immediate news/politics, newspapers are evaluated on their broader educative role — shaping economic and moral understanding — which serves as a criterion for their societal importance.
